html:
The Code of Ur-Nammu is the oldest law code that survives, written in Sumerian around 2100 BCE in the kingdom of Ur III in southern Mesopotamia. It is named after the king Ur-Nammu, though some scholars think his son Shulgi issued it.

It is known only from broken clay tablets copied by later scribes. The first pieces were found at Nippur and identified in 1952 by the Assyriologist Samuel Noah Kramer. More fragments have turned up since, but much of the text is still missing.

It opens with a prologue in which the king says he brought justice to the land, set fair weights and measures, and made sure that orphans were not handed over to the rich, nor widows to the powerful. These are among the earliest recorded promises to protect the weak.

The laws follow an "if this, then that" pattern:

  • Murder, robbery and some other crimes were punished by death.
  • Many injuries, such as breaking a bone or cutting off a foot, were punished with a fine in silver, not with matching harm.
  • Other laws deal with marriage, divorce, slaves and false accusations.

It came about three centuries before the far better known Code of Hammurabi, which used similar forms but more often demanded "an eye for an eye". Together they show a long Mesopotamian tradition of kings publishing laws, written in cuneiform, as proof that they ruled justly.
